newsitem.title: UK: ICCO nations still wrangling over buffer stock money.
newsitem.headline: ICCO nations still wrangling over buffer stock money.

text.p: Cocoa nations, meeting under the umbrella of the International Cocoa Organization (ICCO) this week, have still not resolved their differences over how to share buffer stock profits.
Most members have agreed in principle to set up a special reserve fund for the liquidation of the existing cocoa agreement.
But the sticking point is where should the funding come from.
Producer and consumer delegates are also divided over whether the fund should also be used in plugging the budget shortfalls when lucrative buffer stock sales dry up in March 1998.

Producers, who contributed 80 percent of the buffer stocks through a levy system, say the objective of the reserve fund should solely be the liquidation of the current ICCO agreement and must be funded separately by members' contributions.
They want an estimated $4 million profit to be made on the buffer stock sales distributed back to members according to the proportion of their contribution.
"We should decouple the liquidation of the organization from administrative costs," said Musa Jamil, head of Malaysia's Cocoa Board. "You can't have the fund for two purposes."

Consumers however regard buffer stock profits as a bonus and want to use the revenues in both the liquidation and administrative costs. They object to any increase in annual contributions to the ICCO.

"If that's true then it will cause of a bit of a problem," said Tim Mordan of the UK, consumers' spokesman and chairman of the ICCO executive committee when asked what consumers' reaction would be to producers' idea of decoupling buffer stocks from the liquidation of the agreement.

"We need to know how they (producers) are prepared to finance it (reserve fund). If it is from the contributions, that will be difficult because a lot of consumers are reluctant to see a spike in their contributions," Mordan said.
Consumers have reached a consensus of around three million stg for a reserve fund but producers want a smaller fund just for the liquidation, which the ICCO secretariat estimated at 2.3 million stg.
The issue of how to allocate revenues from the sale of 250,000 tonnes of buffer stocks has been on the ICCO agenda since December.
Brazil had blocked a decision in December saying it had already allocated its share from the buffer stock to the fight against witches' broom, a cocoa killer disease that ravaged its crop.
A consensus is needed for a decision, which must be made before March 1998, delegates said.
